progression.startsWith: More Australians die of cancer each year now than thirty years ago. Yet after allowing for the changing age mix, the cancer death rate is lower. Both statements are true. To see how, you need to know exactly what each disease number measures. So today's question: what do incidence, prevalence and mortality measure?
progression.stopsAfter: matching incidence (new cases in a set time), prevalence (everyone living with the disease at one moment) and mortality (deaths from the disease in a set time) to the questions they answer; defining a case, the population at risk and the time window for each; calculating incidence and mortality as counts ÷ population × 100,000 per year, and prevalence as existing cases ÷ population, as a percentage and per 100,000; explaining that mortality divides by the whole population, not by the people with the disease; explaining why a long-lasting disease has prevalence far above incidence, why a rapidly fatal one does not, and why better treatment can raise prevalence while incidence holds steady; explaining why counts and crude rates mislead when populations differ in size or age, and what an age-standardised rate fixes; converting values to one denominator before comparing; choosing a line graph for change over time and a bar graph for comparing groups, with units on the axis; applying this to two unseen data items.

teaching.task: More Australians die of cancer each year than thirty years ago, yet after allowing for the changing age mix, the cancer death rate has fallen. How can both be true, and what do incidence, prevalence and mortality each measure?
teaching.causalExplanation: You've met two of these with dengue. Incidence counts new cases in a set time, and prevalence counts everyone who has the disease at one moment. Incidence is the tap, prevalence is the tank. Now add a third. Mortality counts deaths from the disease in a set time, mort as in mortuary. So it's how many new cases, how many people living with it, and how many deaths. Every rate needs three things defined. First, what counts as a case, for example a diagnosis confirmed by a doctor. Second, the population at risk: the people who could get the disease. For cervical cancer, that's people with a cervix. Third, the time window: usually a year for incidence and mortality, but a single date for prevalence, because it's a snapshot. Leave any of these vague, and two rates that look alike may not be comparable. Let's work all three for type 2 diabetes in one city of eighty thousand people. In 2025, a hundred and sixty people were newly diagnosed. For incidence, new cases go on top and the population goes underneath, then we multiply by a hundred thousand. A hundred and sixty divided by eighty thousand is zero point zero zero two. Times a hundred thousand, that's two hundred per hundred thousand per year. Sense check: that's two in every thousand people, which fits.
teaching.conversationalApproach: More Australians die of cancer each year now than thirty years ago. You've met two of these with dengue. Every rate needs three things defined. Let's work all three for type 2 diabetes in one city of eighty thousand people. Now prevalence. Third, mortality. Side by side: two hundred new cases, five thousand five hundred living with it, and twenty deaths, all per hundred thousand. Now the hook. To collect these data, use a trusted source such as the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, and check each figure's denominator. Two exam questions. Region X is five hundred and forty over one point two million, times a hundred thousand: forty-five per hundred thousand per year. Second. Incidence stayed steady at about sixty new cases per hundred thousand. So for any disease data, ask three things.
teaching.openingDecision: More Australians die of cancer each year now than thirty years ago. Yet after allowing for the changing age mix, the cancer death rate is lower. Both statements are true. To see how, you need to know exactly what each disease number measures. So today's question: what do incidence, prevalence and mortality measure?
teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. In 2024, Region X, with one point two million people, recorded five hundred and forty new lung cancer cases. Region Y, with three hundred thousand people, recorded one hundred and eighty. Calculate the incidence in each region per hundred thousand. Region Y's population is much older. Explain why these rates can't show which region's people are at greater risk. Pause here to answer. Second. The table shows incidence, mortality and prevalence for a non-infectious disease in Australia in 2005, 2015 and 2025, each per hundred thousand people. Describe the trend in each measure. Then suggest an explanation for the rise in prevalence that fits the table. Pause here to answer.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ2-02 (p 57): "collect and represent data to show the incidence, prevalence and mortality rates of non-infectious diseases, for example:" with "nutritional diseases" and "diseases caused by environmental exposure" (scenes 4 to 6 and 9, type 2 diabetes as the nutritional example; attempt 1, lung cancer as the environmental example). B8-IQ3-01 (p 57): "analyse patterns of non-infectious diseases in populations, including their incidence and prevalence, including but not limited to:" with the same two examples (scenes 7 and 8, attempt 2). Inquiry questions: "Do non-infectious diseases cause more deaths than infectious diseases?" and "Why are epidemiological studies used?" (the hook and scene 8 show why careful measurement matters; b11 answers the second fully).

design.visualSystem: One coded data board fills the frame: a task strip at the top (the short task in plain words), the equation on its own line below it, and a grouped givens panel at the left, each value with its unit. Working writes one stage at a time at the right; a result stays only while the next step uses it. A three-column measures bar sits along the bottom from scene 2 to scene 9: "incidence: new cases", "prevalence: living with it", "mortality: deaths", each lighting when used and filling with its worked value from scenes 4 to 6. Painted thumbnails appear small and only where they carry the disease (m8-pancreas-v1.png for type 2 diabetes, m8-lungs-healthy-v1.png for lung cancer); populations are bars and pyramids, never figures. At most three bright text items; earlier lines dim to grey.
